procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated July 29, 1971, by the State Government confirming the detention order under s. 12 of the West Bengal Prevention of Violent Activities Act, 1970.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The text does not mention any High Court proceedings. The petitioner directly filed a writ petition in the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner filed a writ petition in the Supreme Court under Article 32 of the Constitution of India, seeking a writ in the nature of habeas corpus. The petition was ultimately dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether grounds not raised in a habeas corpus petition can be urged for the first time during arguments before the Court.

facts: The petitioner sent a habeas corpus petition from jail.
During the hearing, the petitioner's counsel raised two additional grounds that were not included in the original petition.
law: Ordinarily, the Court does not permit grounds to be raised during arguments if they were not included in the written petition.
application: The Court decided to make an exception to its ordinary rule in this case.

The Court reasoned that since this was a habeas corpus petition, which concerns a person's liberty, and because the petitioner had made the petition himself from jail, it was appropriate to allow the new grounds to be raised.
reasoning.conclusion: The Court allowed the new grounds to be argued, even though they were not in the original petition, because of the special nature of a habeas corpus case and the fact that the petitioner had filed it from jail.

issue.issue_text: Whether a delay of 34 days by the government in considering the petitioner's representation was so inordinate as to invalidate the detention.

facts: The petitioner's representation was received by the State Government on May 27, 1971.
The government considered and rejected the representation on July 1, 1971, after a delay of 34 days.
On June 7, 1971, the government sent the petitioner's case file and representation to the Advisory Board.
The government considered the representation as soon as it was returned from the Board.
law: The law requires the government to afford a detenu the earliest opportunity to make a representation against their detention order.
There is no hard and fast rule regarding what constitutes an inordinate delay; each case must be decided on its own facts.
application: The Court found that most of the 34-day delay was explained by the fact that the petitioner's representation and case record were with the Advisory Board.
The Court rejected the argument that the government should have decided the matter in the 11 days before sending the file to the Board (May 27 to June 7).

It reasoned that the government may need time to make proper inquiries, especially when the detention order was passed by a different authority (the District Magistrate), which could involve investigating the local situation and the detenu's history.
The Court also noted that the petitioner had not initially raised the issue of delay in his petition, which is why the government's affidavit did not offer an explanation.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that, in the specific circumstances of this case, the 34-day delay was not so inordinate as to invalidate the petitioner's detention.

issue.issue_text: Whether the petitioner's acts of mischief by fire and explosive substance on an educational institution's property disturbed or were likely to disturb public order.

facts: The petitioner was accused of two separate acts of arson at the Moynaguri Higher Secondary School.
In the first incident, the petitioner and others set fire to books, registers, and furniture in the Headmaster's room and then placed a bomb on the school premises.
In the second incident, the petitioner and others again set fire to parts of the school and threatened the staff with death if they resisted or reported the incident.
law: The relevant law, the West Bengal Prevention of Violent Activities Act, 1970, distinguishes between simple mischief by fire on an educational institution's property and mischief of the same nature that "disturbs or is likely to disturb public order."
The court uses the test of whether the acts disturb "the even tempo of the life of the community of that specified locality."
application: The Court reasoned that the petitioner's actions were not simple vandalism but were intended to achieve a larger, more disruptive goal.
The object was to disrupt the school's functioning by destroying its records and, more importantly, to create a widespread scare.
The Court inferred that this scare would prevent teaching staff and pupils from daring to attend the school and would make parents afraid to send their children there for fear of them being harmed.
The placement of a bomb after the fire had already been set was seen as clear evidence of the intent to create this terror and disrupt community life.
Therefore, the Court found that the acts had a greater "potentiality" than simple mischief and were specifically aimed at disturbing the community's normal routine and sense of security.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the petitioner's acts of arson and intimidation were not merely mischief but constituted acts that disturbed or were likely to disturb public order. The Court found that the intent to create a scare and disrupt the functioning of the school directly affected the "even tempo" of the community, thus justifying the detention under the Act.

issue.issue_text: Whether vague allegations by the petitioner are sufficient to challenge the detention order when the Advisory Board has found sufficient material justifying it.

facts: The petitioner made allegations challenging their detention order.
The petitioner's case, along with their representation and other materials, was placed before an Advisory Board.
The Advisory Board reviewed the case and reported that there was sufficient material to justify the detention order.
law: A court cannot accept allegations that are vague, indefinite, and not supported by any material or specific details.
application: The Court found that the allegations made by the petitioner were vague and not backed by any definite material.
The Court contrasted the petitioner's unsubstantiated claims with the formal report of the Advisory Board, which had reviewed all the materials and found sufficient cause for the detention.
In the absence of any definite material from the petitioner, the Court deferred to the findings of the Advisory Board.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's challenge, holding that vague and unsupported allegations are insufficient to overturn a detention order, particularly when an Advisory Board has reviewed the case and found sufficient material to justify it.

arguments.issue_text: Whether grounds not raised in a habeas corpus petition can be urged for the first time during arguments before the Court.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner's counsel sought to raise two additional grounds during oral arguments which were not included in the original habeas corpus petition filed from jail.
respondent_arguments: Ordinarily, a petitioner should not be permitted to raise grounds that were not included in the written petition.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a delay of 34 days by the government in considering the petitioner's representation was so inordinate as to invalidate the detention.
appellant_arguments: The delay in considering the petitioner's representation was inordinate and therefore violated Article 22(5) of the Constitution.
respondent_arguments: The State produced records and notings from the case file to justify the time taken to consider the representation.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the petitioner's acts of mischief by fire and explosive substance on an educational institution's property disturbed or were likely to disturb public order.
appellant_arguments: The grounds furnished to the detenu, concerning his acts, did not constitute a breach of public order, and therefore, the detention was illegal.
respondent_arguments: The petitioner's acts justified the detention order, implying they constituted a breach of public order. (Inferred from the State's action of issuing and confirming the detention order).

arguments.issue_text: Whether vague allegations by the petitioner are sufficient to challenge the detention order when the Advisory Board has found sufficient material justifying it.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner denied the allegations made against him in his habeas corpus petition.
respondent_arguments: The petitioner's case, along with his representation, was placed before the Advisory Board, which found sufficient material to justify the detention, making the petitioner's denials insufficient.

cases.principle: The distinction between 'law and order' and 'public order' is one of degree and the extent of the reach of the act in question upon society. Acts similar in nature, but committed in different contexts and circumstances, might affect law and order in one case and public order in another.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An appropriate authority is bound to provide a detenu an opportunity to make a representation and must consider it as early as possible. However, no hard and fast rule can be laid down regarding the permissible time for consideration; whether a delay is inordinate enough to invalidate the detention must be determined on the facts of each individual case. Vague and indefinite allegations by a petitioner, unsupported by material particulars, are not sufficient to challenge a detention order.
obiter: In considering a representation, the government may need to make inquiries as to the situation in the locality, the circumstances under which detention was found necessary, and the previous history of the person detained, which can justify the time taken.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court dismissed the habeas corpus petition, concluding that the petitioner's acts of arson and placing a bomb at an educational institution were not mere mischief but constituted a disturbance of public order. The court reasoned that the object of the acts was to create a scare, disrupt the school's functioning, and terrorize students, staff, and parents, thereby disturbing the even tempo of community life. Additionally, the court found that a 34-day delay by the government in considering the petitioner's representation was not inordinate under the circumstances, as time was required for inquiries and the case file was with the Advisory Board for a portion of that period.
legal_tests_applied: The distinction between 'law and order' and 'public order' is one of degree and the extent of the breach upon society; for an act to affect 'public order,' it must affect the community at large.
An act disturbs public order if it disturbs 'the even tempo of the life of the community of that specified locality.'
There is no hard and fast rule regarding the time which can be taken by the government to consider a detenu's representation; each case must be decided on its own facts.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that his acts were merely a 'law and order' issue failed because the court found the acts were 'different in potentiality' from simple arson. The court determined the object was 'vandalism, to disrupt its working by burning its records and to create a scare so that neither the teaching staff nor the pupils would dare attend it for prosecution of studies,' which constituted a disturbance of public order.

The appellant's challenge based on the 34-day delay in considering his representation was rejected because the court held that 'each case must be decided on i\is own facts' and found the delay was not inordinate, partly because 'the representation and the record remained with the Board' and the government needed time to make inquiries.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position that the detention was justified to maintain public order succeeded because the court agreed that the petitioner's acts, in their specific context, were likely to disturb public order. The court reasoned that targeting an educational institution to create fear among staff, pupils, and parents 'disturbed or was likely to disturb the even tempo of the community in that particular locality.'

The respondent's justification for the 34-day delay was accepted, as the court acknowledged that the government 'might have to make inquiries as to the situation in the locality, the nature of and the circumstances ia which detention was found necessarV' and that part of the delay was explained by the Advisory Board's review process.
policy_considerations: While ordinarily new grounds cannot be raised for the first time during arguments, the court made an exception because 'this was a habeas corpus petition and, furthermore, made by the petitioner from jail,' showing special latitude in matters concerning personal liberty.
